newsitem.title: FRANCE: TENNIS-NOAH'S LEADERSHIP SKILLS PUT TO TEST AGAIN.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-NOAH'S LEADERSHIP SKILLS PUT TO TEST AGAIN.

text.p: Yannick Noah's proven ability to inspire team spirit will be put to the test for the second time in five years this weekend.
The natural leader of French tennis since he won the French Open in 1983, Noah guided Guy Forget and Henri Leconte to Davis Cup victory over the United States in 1991.
Now he is mentor to a new generation represented by Cedric Pioline and Arnaud Boetsch, who will tackle Sweden's Stefan Edberg and Thomas Enqvist in Malmo.
The 1996 team has much in common with the 1991 combination. Once again the French are underdogs and once again they rely on Noah's leadership skills.
Forget, who should again anchor France's doubles team, evoked the atmosphere before the crucial match won by Pioline against Italian Renzo Furlan in this year's semifinals.
"Before the match, Cedric took our hands and held them tight. Emotions were showing on his face and you could tell how badly he wanted to win," he said.
Pioline has long been the odd man out in the French team.
Whereas Noah, Leconte, Forget or Boetsch are products of the ambitious scouting programme launched by the French Federation 20 years ago, Pioline is a self-made player.
And relations at first were so tense that the former U.S. Open finalist was left out of the team until 1994.
"At the time, I told him there was a spirit in the team and he did not have it. I thought this guy had a personality but he was not one of us," Noah said.
Forget was even harsher. "I think we should forget about Pioline making it into the team. He is hostile to any sort of cooperation between players."
But when Pioline made it to the world's top 10, it became difficult to leave him out.
Boetsch said he had a long talk with Pioline in Marseille in 1994 to let him know he was willing to cooperate.
Other team members were more reluctant until Pioline parted with then coach Henri Dumont, thought to be responsible for the player's individualism.
"Today, everything's great. It was nonsense. Pioline was under Dumont's influence," said Forget.
Healing the rift with Pioline was the first step towards rebuilding a competitive team but results did not come immediately.
After leaving Dumont Pioline, who had at his best reached number nine in the world rankings, endured hard times and slumped to 51st at the end of 1994.

In the same time, Boestch, who had made it into the top 20 in 1993, also sank in the following season while Forget was trying to stage an unlikely comeback after spending one year away from courts with a knee injury.
For the first time this season France have had their best players in form simultaneously.
Boetsch and Pioline have returned into the ATP Tour's top 20, while Forget and Guillaume Raoux have become a solid doubles team.
